title: Chapter 10: Candle Magic
md:
Candle magic is the heart of AMY: you give an intention a body of wax, a voice of flame and a span of time, and you stay with it while it burns.

### Choosing the candle

- **Tealights and chime candles** burn for one to two hours. Good for a single session.
- **Tapers and pillars** can be relit over several nights.
- **Seven-day glass candles**, also called vigil or novena candles, are the botanica standard. In AMY they are lit in nightly sessions over seven nights, never left burning.
- **Figure candles** shaped like people, hearts or houses exist in folk practice. AMY uses them only for self-work and the home.
- **Diyas**, small clay lamps with ghee or oil, carry Hindu devotion.

Choose the color by Chapter 9, or simply use white, which serves every purpose.

### Preparing the candle

1. **Cleanse it.** Wipe it with a cloth dampened with salt water or holy water, or pass it through incense smoke.
2. **Carve it.** With a pin or toothpick, carve your name, initials, a word for your intention, a symbol or a sigil into the wax. On a glass candle, write on the glass or on a label instead.
3. **Dress it.** Rub a few drops of oil onto the candle. To draw something toward you, stroke from the top toward the middle and from the bottom toward the middle, or toward yourself. To send something away, stroke from the middle outward, or away from yourself. On a glass candle, make three small holes in the top of the wax with a skewer, add three drops of oil, and sprinkle a very small pinch of finely ground herb. Too much herb will flare.
4. **Load the intention.** Hold the candle in both hands. Speak your intention aloud, in the present tense, as if it is already unfolding.
5. **Pray over it** in your tradition, or simply breathe with it three times.

### The petition

Write your intention on a small square of paper. Fold it toward you to draw in, away from you to release. Place it under the candle holder or plate, never under a glass candle directly where heat collects. Many practitioners write the petition three times, crossing the last with their full name.

### Lighting and the session

1. Set the candle on a heat-safe plate, away from anything that can burn.
2. Light it with a match, saying a short blessing.
3. Read the intention aloud. Pray, meditate, or simply sit and watch the flame.
4. Stay with it for the whole session: fifteen to thirty minutes is typical.
5. End by snuffing or covering the flame. Many traditions avoid blowing out a sacred flame, so as not to scatter the prayer. Say a closing word: Amen, Om Shanti, or And so it is.
6. Relight the next night. Never leave the candle burning while you sleep or leave the room.

### Reading the flame

Practitioners have long watched how a flame behaves as a sign of how the work is moving. These are traditional readings, offered for reflection.

| What you see | Traditional reading |
| --- | --- |
| Tall, steady, bright flame | The work is strong and unobstructed |
| Small, weak or low flame | Resistance, or energy is low; be patient, consider repeating the work |
| Flame that flickers or dances with no draft | Spirit is present; strong feeling around the matter |
| Crackling or popping | Something is trying to communicate; or there is conflict around the matter |
| Flame that leans toward you | The work is coming toward you |
| Flame that leans away | The work is going out into the world, or something is pulling away |
| Two flames, or a split wick | Another person or a second matter is involved |
| Black smoke | Heaviness or obstacles being burned away |
| White smoke | Blessing, purity, prayers rising |
| Flame goes out on its own | The work is finished, or blocked; relight once with a prayer |

**Before you read, rule out the ordinary:** drafts, a long untrimmed wick, too much oil or herb, and the shape of the vessel all change a flame. Trim wicks to about a quarter inch.

### Reading the glass of a seven-day candle

When the candle has finished its last session and the glass is completely cool, look at it from the side and from above.

| What the glass shows | Traditional reading |
| --- | --- |
| Clean, clear glass | The work went smoothly; the way is open |
| Black soot at the top only | Early resistance that was cleared |
| Black soot at the bottom only | Resistance near the end, or the matter needs more work |
| Black soot all over | Heavy obstacles, or much was absorbed; many practitioners follow with a cleansing |
| White or grey haze | Spiritual help was present; peace; sometimes confusion to be clarified |
| Soot on one side | Energy or resistance coming from one direction or one person |
| Wax left at the bottom | Something unfinished; look at what remains in the matter |
| Wax burned evenly to the base | The work is complete |
| Images in the soot | Read them as symbols, the way one reads clouds |
| Cracked or broken glass | Traditionally a sign of strong opposition, or a protective candle taking a blow; practically, a safety hazard. Stop at once and dispose of it safely |

In AMY, the seeker photographs the cooled glass on the eighth day. AMY offers a first look, and a human reader can study it in depth.

### Reading wax in water (ceromancy)

Drip melted wax from a candle into a bowl of cold water and read the shapes it forms. Hearts, rings, birds, doors and roads each suggest their meanings. This old divination is popular on Samhain and New Year's Eve.

### Disposing of the remains

When the work is finished, throw away candle remains, petitions and spent herbs in the trash, bury biodegradable remains in the earth, or, for release work, take them away from the house. Wash the glass candle jar with hot soapy water if you wish to reuse it, or recycle it.

title: Chapter 11: Cleansing, Protection, Love, Prosperity and the Open Road
md:
Most of what people bring to AMY falls into five kinds of work: clearing what is heavy, guarding what is precious, opening the heart, inviting abundance, and opening a blocked path. Begin almost every working with a cleansing.

### Cleansing

Cleansing removes heaviness from a person, a space or an object before new work begins.

- **Smoke cleansing.** Burn a small bundle of rosemary, bay, cedar or garden sage, or a stick of frankincense, in a fireproof dish. Carry the smoke through each room clockwise, opening a window to let the old air out. Pass the smoke around your body from head to feet. (In many Native nations, burning white sage is a ceremony called smudging; AMY uses other herbs out of respect.)
- **Salt.** Dissolve a spoon of salt in a bowl of water and wipe doorknobs, windowsills and mirrors. Or sprinkle salt in the corners of a room overnight and sweep it out in the morning.
- **Floor wash.** A botanica and rootwork tradition. Add a little salt, a splash of vinegar or lemon juice, and a cooled herbal tea (rosemary, basil, lemongrass) to a bucket of water. Wash the floor from the back of the house to the front door, then pour the water out toward the street.
- **Spiritual bath for the hands and feet.** Steep rosemary, rose petals and a pinch of salt in hot water, let it cool, and pour it over your hands and feet while praying. AMY avoids full-body herbal baths because of skin sensitivity.
- **Sound.** Ring a bell, clap in each corner, or play a singing bowl to break up stagnant energy.
- **The egg limpia.** The curandera's cleansing, with its timing in Chapter 14 and its full steps in the AMY Lovable Build Pack.
- **Holy water and prayer.** Sprinkle holy water in each room with the sign of the cross, or chant in each room in your tradition.

### Protection

Protection builds a boundary around you, your home and the people you love.

- **Threshold salt.** A line of salt inside the front door.
- **The witch bottle.** An old English and American charm. A jar holding salt, rosemary, a few bent nails or pins and a little vinegar is sealed and buried near the door or hidden in the house, to catch and hold any harm sent your way. AMY's version omits bodily fluids, which old recipes used.
- **Mirrors.** A small mirror facing outward in a window reflects ill will back to its source. Many traditions place a mirror near the entrance.
- **The evil eye charm.** The blue nazar from the Mediterranean and Middle East, the red horn (cornicello) of Italy, the hamsa, and in India the lemon and seven chilies over the door or a black dot on a child.
- **Saint Michael.** Catholic practitioners pray to Saint Michael the Archangel and keep his image near the door. The Saint Michael candle burns on Tuesdays.
- **Hanuman.** In Hindu devotion, reciting the Hanuman Chalisa on Tuesdays and Saturdays is a beloved protection.
- **Visualization.** Imagine a sphere of white or gold light around you, sealed above and below. See Chapter 16 for the shielding meditation.
- **Red thread.** A red thread tied on the left wrist protects in Jewish folk practice (often from Rachel's Tomb), in Hindu puja (kalava), and in many Latin American homes for babies.

### Love

AMY's love work begins with the seeker's own heart. It calls in love that is freely given and never targets a specific person's will.

- **Self-love first.** A pink candle, rose quartz and a mirror. Say aloud three things you love about yourself on each of seven nights.
- **Calling in a partner.** On a Friday under a waxing moon, write the qualities of the love you want (not a name) on a petition, dress a pink candle with rose oil, and keep the petition in a sachet of rose petals and lavender afterward.
- **Honey jar for sweetness.** A rootwork classic. Write a petition for sweetness between you and someone you already share love with, fold it toward you, place it in a jar of honey, and taste a drop while saying: as this honey is sweet to me, may our words be sweet to each other. Burn a small candle on the lid on Fridays. AMY uses honey jars only for existing relationships with goodwill on both sides, family peace, and workplace harmony.
- **Reconciliation.** Two candles, one for each person, moved a little closer together each night for seven nights while praying for peace and honest speech, not for the other person's surrender.
- **Healing a broken heart.** A white candle, rose petals in water, Release in Water under a waning moon.

### Prosperity

- **The bay leaf wish** on a Thursday under a waxing moon.
- **Cinnamon at the door** on the first of the month.
- **The money bowl.** A bowl holding a few coins, a bay leaf, a cinnamon stick, rice and a citrine or pyrite. Add a coin each week while naming one thing you are grateful for.
- **Green candle work** on Thursdays, dressed with patchouli or basil oil.
- **Lakshmi's lamp** on Friday at dusk, and a clean, well-lit home on Diwali.
- **Saint Joseph** for work and home in Catholic practice; **Saint Expedite** in some botanica traditions for quick results.

### Opening the road

Road opening, called *abre camino* in botanica tradition, clears blocks so opportunities can reach you.

1. Cleanse yourself and your home first.
2. Under a new or waxing moon, ideally on a Thursday, dress a Road Opener candle (or a Ganesha candle for Hindu devotees) with Road Opener oil.
3. Write on a petition the doors you want opened: a job, a sale, a decision, a meeting.
4. Light the candle each night for seven nights. Each night name one action you will take the next day, and take it.
5. Sweep your front step outward on the first morning and inward on the last.
6. Read the glass on the eighth day.

In Hindu devotion, begin any new venture by worshipping Ganesha, offering durva grass and modak, and chanting Om Gam Ganapataye Namah.

title: Chapter 12: Divination
md:
Divination is the art of asking a question and reading the answer in a symbol: a card, a flame, a shape in water. In AMY it is a tool for reflection, not a fixed prediction, and readings are offered for entertainment and reflection.

### How to ask a good question

- Ask open questions: "What do I need to understand about my work?" rather than "Will I get the job?"
- Ask about yourself, not about what another person is secretly thinking.
- Ask once. Asking the same question again and again clouds the answer.
- Write the question down before you begin, and the answer after.

### Tarot

The tarot deck has 78 cards. The 22 cards of the **Major Arcana** describe the great passages of a life. The 56 cards of the **Minor Arcana** describe daily events in four suits: Wands (fire: will, work, passion), Cups (water: feeling, love, relationships), Swords (air: thought, conflict, truth) and Pentacles (earth: money, body, home). Each suit runs from Ace to Ten, then Page, Knight, Queen and King.

| Card | Upright meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 The Fool | A new beginning, trust, a leap |
| I The Magician | Will, skill, having what you need |
| II The High Priestess | Intuition, mystery, inner knowing |
| III The Empress | Abundance, nurture, creativity |
| IV The Emperor | Structure, authority, protection |
| V The Hierophant | Tradition, teaching, faith |
| VI The Lovers | Love, a choice made with the whole heart |
| VII The Chariot | Movement through will, victory |
| VIII Strength | Gentle courage, patience |
| IX The Hermit | Solitude, seeking, inner light |
| X Wheel of Fortune | Cycles, change, turning points |
| XI Justice | Truth, fairness, consequences |
| XII The Hanged Man | Surrender, a new perspective, pause |
| XIII Death | Endings that make way for beginnings (rarely literal) |
| XIV Temperance | Balance, healing, the right measure |
| XV The Devil | Attachment, habit, what binds you |
| XVI The Tower | Sudden change, revelation, breaking open |
| XVII The Star | Hope, renewal, guidance |
| XVIII The Moon | Dreams, uncertainty, the unconscious |
| XIX The Sun | Joy, clarity, success |
| XX Judgement | Awakening, calling, forgiveness |
| XXI The World | Completion, wholeness, arrival |

**Spreads.** One card for the day. Three cards for situation, advice and likely direction, or past, present and next. The Celtic Cross uses ten positions for a deep reading of one matter.

**Other decks.** Oracle decks have no fixed structure and carry their own guidebooks. The Lenormand deck has 36 simple picture cards read in combinations. Affirmation and scripture card decks, like the ones AMY plans to create, offer a word or verse for the day.

### The pendulum

Hold a weighted pendulum or a ring on a thread still between your fingers. Ask it to show you yes, then no, then maybe. Then ask simple yes or no questions. Keep your hand still and your mind open. Pendulums are best for small choices and for finding lost objects over a map.

### Scrying

Scrying is gazing into a surface until images arise in the mind.

- **Water.** A dark bowl of water, lit by a single candle behind you. The Italian spell of the carafe from Chapter 2 was a form of water scrying.
- **Black mirror.** A mirror painted black on the back, or an obsidian disc.
- **Fire.** Watching the flame of a candle or a hearth fire.
- **Crystal.** A clear quartz sphere.

Relax your eyes, breathe slowly, and let impressions come for ten to twenty minutes. Write down everything without judging it.

### Reading water, wax, eggs and matches

| Method | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Matches in water | Seven lit matches dropped in a glass of water; how they float, sink, gather or cross speaks to the question |
| Wax in water | Melted wax dripped into cold water forms shapes to read |
| Egg in water | An egg used in a limpia is cracked into water; bubbles, threads, cloudiness and spots are read |
| Egg white in water | Folk divination on Saint John's Eve or Midsummer: an egg white in a glass of water left in the sun forms shapes |
| Oil in water | Italian malocchio diagnosis: drops of olive oil in a bowl of water; if they spread or break apart, the evil eye is present, and a prayer is said to lift it |

### Tea leaves and coffee grounds

Tasseography reads the shapes left in a cup. Drink loose-leaf tea or thick Turkish or Greek coffee, leaving a little liquid. Swirl three times, turn the cup over on the saucer, wait, then read the shapes from the rim (near future) to the bottom (further off).

### Opening the book

Bibliomancy is opening a holy book at random and reading the first verse your eye falls on as guidance. Christians have done this with the Bible for centuries, and it is done with the Psalms, the Bhagavad Gita and books of poetry. AMY offers a digital version from the Wisdom Library.

### Runes and the I Ching

- **Runes.** The 24 letters of the Elder Futhark alphabet, carved on stones or wood and drawn from a bag. Each has a name and meaning, such as Fehu for wealth and Algiz for protection.
- **The I Ching.** The Chinese Book of Changes: three coins tossed six times build one of 64 hexagrams, each with a text of guidance.

### Signs and dreams

Repeating numbers, a song returning at the right moment, a bird at the window, a name heard three times in a day, a vivid dream: many seekers experience the world as speaking to them. AMY invites them to write these signs down and look for patterns over time, rather than reading too much into any single one. A dream journal by the bed is the simplest divination tool there is.

title: Chapter 13: Spellcraft: Building a Working of Your Own
md:
Every ritual in every tradition shares the same bones: an intention, a time, a space made sacred, an action, a release and a return. Learn the bones and you can build your own.

### The anatomy of a working

1. **Intention.** Write one sentence, in the present tense, about your own life. "I am finding work that respects my gifts."
2. **Timing.** Choose the moon phase, day and hour from Part Two. If the need is urgent, now is the right time.
3. **Materials.** Choose a candle color, an herb, a stone, or simply a glass of water. Fewer, meaningful materials are better than many.
4. **Cleansing.** Cleanse yourself, the space and the materials.
5. **Opening the space.** Mark the beginning: cast a circle, make the sign of the cross, perform achamana with a sip of water and state your sankalpa, or simply light the candle and say, "I begin."
6. **The act.** Carve, dress and light the candle; write and fold the petition; tie the knots; fill the jar.
7. **Raising energy.** Chant, pray, breathe deeply, hum, drum or visualize the outcome until you feel full of the intention.
8. **Release.** Let it go into the flame, the water or the earth. Say Amen, Om Shanti, So mote it be, or And so it is.
9. **Closing and grounding.** Thank whoever you called on. Close the circle. Eat something, touch the ground, wash your hands.
10. **Action.** Take one ordinary step toward the intention within a day.
11. **Record.** Write it in your Book of Shadows.

### Opening and closing in different traditions

- **Wiccan circle.** Walk the edge of your space clockwise three times, imagining a circle of light. Face east, south, west and north in turn, greeting air, fire, water and earth. At the end, thank each direction in reverse and walk the circle counterclockwise to open it.
- **Christian.** Make the sign of the cross, pray the Our Father or the Prayer to Saint Michael, and close with the Glory Be.
- **Hindu.** Sip water three times (achamana), state your name, the date and your purpose (sankalpa), invoke Ganesha first, and close with aarti and a prayer for forgiveness of any error in the worship.
- **Open.** Three slow breaths, a word of intention, and a word of thanks at the end.

### Sigils

A sigil is a symbol you design to carry a single intention, a method made popular by the artist Austin Osman Spare.

1. Write your intention as a short sentence: "I AM CALM AND CONFIDENT."
2. Cross out repeating letters, then the vowels. You are left with a few consonants.
3. Combine those letters into one design, overlapping and stylizing them until the words can no longer be read.
4. Charge it: gaze at it while breathing deeply, or carve it into a candle.
5. Let it go: burn it safely, bury it or tuck it away, and stop thinking about it.

### Knot magic

Take a cord the color of your intention. Tie nine knots along it while chanting a short verse, each knot sealing the intention a little more. Keep the cord until the intention is fulfilled, then untie the knots or bury it. Knot work is for your own goals, never for tying up another person.

### Jars, sachets and bags

- **Intention jar.** A small jar layered with salt, herbs, a stone, a petition and a sealing candle on the lid. Protection jars sit by the door; money jars by the place you work.
- **Sachet.** A small cloth pouch of dried herbs and a stone, carried in a pocket or tucked under a pillow. Lavender and chamomile for sleep; basil and a coin for money; rosemary and salt for protection.
- **Mojo bag.** In Hoodoo, a mojo or gris-gris bag is a red flannel bag holding roots, herbs, stones and personal items, prepared and fed with oil or whiskey. It is a living part of the tradition, and AMY recommends learning it from a rootworker.

### Working with the ancestors

Almost every culture honors those who came before. An ancestor altar holds photographs of the departed, a glass of fresh water, a white candle, and small offerings of what they loved: coffee, bread, a flower, a sweet. Speak to them by name. Tell them your news. Ask for their guidance and protection. Change the water every few days.

The ancestor altar is traditionally for those who have passed. Photographs of the living are not placed there.

Hindu devotees offer food, water and sesame to the ancestors during Pitru Paksha and on Amavasya. Catholics pray for the Holy Souls, especially in November. Día de los Muertos builds an ofrenda with marigolds, candles and pan de muerto.

### Kitchen craft

- **Simmer pots.** Water with orange peel, cinnamon and clove for warmth and prosperity; lemon, rosemary and bay for clearing; rose petals and vanilla for love. Never leave a simmering pot unattended.
- **Intention cooking.** Stir clockwise to draw in, counterclockwise to release. Speak a blessing over bread before it rises.
- **Salt and bread** are the oldest gifts for a new home.

### Dream work

Keep a notebook by the bed. Before sleep, hold a question in your mind and ask for a dream about it. On waking, write before you move. A small sachet of lavender under the pillow helps many people sleep. (Mugwort is often used for dreams but is not safe in pregnancy and should never be swallowed.)

### When a working does not seem to work

- Look again: the answer may have come in a different form than expected.
- Check the intention: was it about your own life? Was it clear?
- Check the action: did you take the ordinary steps?
- Wait a full moon cycle before repeating it.
- Ask whether the outcome you wanted was truly the one you needed. Sometimes a closed door is protection.

title: Chapter 14: A Grimoire of Rituals, With the Right Time for Each
md:
This grimoire gives every AMY ritual its best timing at a glance, then the full steps for the rituals not already written out in the AMY Lovable Build Pack. Flame is always attended, and every candle session ends with the flame put out.

### The timing table

| Ritual | For | Best moon | Best day | Best time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Matches in Water | Any question | Any | Any | Evening |
| Bay Leaf Wish | Money, wishes | New or waxing | Thursday | Evening |
| Salt at the Threshold | Protection | Waning or full | Saturday (Catholic: Tuesday) | Sunset |
| A Glass for the Ancestors | Family, remembrance | Waning or new | Monday (Hindu: Saturday, Amavasya) | Evening |
| Cinnamon at the Door | Money | Any | First day of the month | Morning |
| Rosemary Clarity Rinse | Purpose, clarity | Waxing or new | Wednesday | Morning |
| Rose Petal Heart Bowl | Love | Waxing | Friday | Evening |
| Full Moon Water | Gratitude, peace | Full | Any | Night |
| New Moon Intention Paper | Beginnings | New | Any | Evening |
| Release in Water | Letting go | Waning | Saturday | Evening |
| Egg Cleansing (Limpia) | Protection, cleansing | Waning | Tuesday or Friday | Evening |
| Sunday Morning Light | Purpose, courage | Any | Sunday | Sunrise |
| Ghee Diya for Lakshmi | Abundance | Waxing or full | Friday, Purnima | Sunset |
| Ganesha Durva Offering | Obstacles | Waxing | Tuesday or Wednesday, Chaturthi | Morning |
| Saint Michael Tuesday Prayer | Protection | Any | Tuesday, Sept 29 | Evening |
| Holy Souls Monday Light | The departed | Any | Monday, November | Evening |
| The Witch Bottle | Protecting the home | Waning or full | Saturday | Evening |
| The Money Bowl | Steady abundance | New, then weekly | Thursday | Morning |
| Honey Jar for Peace | Sweetness in a family or team | Waxing | Friday | Evening |
| Seven Nights in the Mirror | Self-love | Waxing | Begin on a Friday | Night |
| The Nine-Knot Cord | A personal goal | Waxing | Sunday or Thursday | Any |
| Bread and Salt for a New Home | Blessing a home | Any | The day you move in | Morning |
| Epiphany Door Blessing | Blessing the home for the year | Any | January 6 | Daytime |
| Candlemas Candle Blessing | Blessing the year's candles | Any | February 2 | Daytime |
| Oil and Water for the Evil Eye | Lifting envy and heaviness | Waning | Tuesday or Friday | Any |
| The Silent Supper | The ancestors | Any | Samhain or All Souls | Night |
| Diwali Lamps | Light, Lakshmi, new beginnings | New moon of Kartika | Diwali night | Dusk |
| New Year Wax Reading | Guidance for the year | Any | New Year's Eve | Midnight |
| Seven-day candle Light Work (each candle) | See Chapter 10 and the Build Pack | Per candle | Per candle | The seeker's chosen evening hour |

### The Witch Bottle

*Materials:* a small glass jar with a lid, coarse salt, a sprig of rosemary, three to nine bent nails or pins, a little vinegar, a black or white candle.

1. Under a waning or full moon on a Saturday, cleanse the jar.
2. Add salt, rosemary and the bent nails, saying: whatever is sent against this house is caught, held and turned to nothing.
3. Pour in vinegar to cover, and close the lid tightly.
4. Drip wax from the candle around the lid to seal it. Put out the candle.
5. Bury the jar near your front door, or hide it in a high cupboard near the entrance.
6. Tell AMY where it rests, and renew it once a year.

### The Money Bowl

*Materials:* a small bowl, a handful of rice, three coins, a bay leaf, a cinnamon stick, a citrine or pyrite (optional), a green candle.

1. On a Thursday after the new moon, place the rice in the bowl and set the coins, bay leaf, cinnamon and stone on top.
2. Light the green candle beside it and say what you are grateful to already have.
3. Each Thursday, add one coin and name one new thing you are thankful for.
4. At the end of each month, give the coins to someone in need, and begin again.

### Honey Jar for Peace

*Materials:* a small jar of honey, a paper and pen, a pinch of lavender and rose, a small white or pink candle.

1. On a Friday under a waxing moon, write the names of the family or team, and beneath them: may our words be sweet, may we understand each other.
2. Fold the paper toward you and push it into the honey with the herbs.
3. Taste a drop of honey from your finger and say: as this honey is sweet to me, may we be sweet to one another.
4. Close the jar and light the small candle on the lid. Stay with it until it burns out or end the session safely.
5. Repeat the candle each Friday.

AMY uses honey jars only where goodwill is shared, never to sway a person against their will.

### Seven Nights in the Mirror

1. Beginning on a Friday under a waxing moon, light a pink candle in front of a mirror.
2. Look into your own eyes and say three things you love or respect about yourself, different each night.
3. Say: I am worthy of love that is freely given.
4. Sit for three minutes, then put out the candle.
5. On the seventh night, write the twenty-one things on a card and keep it.

### The Nine-Knot Cord

1. On a Sunday or Thursday under a waxing moon, take a cord the color of your goal.
2. Tie nine knots, saying with each: by knot of one, the work's begun; by knot of two, it shall come true; and so on through nine, or a prayer of your own for each.
3. Keep the cord on your altar. When the goal is reached, untie it with thanks.

### Bread and Salt for a New Home

1. On the day you move in, carry a loaf of bread and a dish of salt across the threshold before anything else.
2. Say: may this house never know hunger, and may it never lack flavor and peace.
3. Light a white candle in the kitchen and walk through every room with a blessing.
4. Share the bread with the first people who visit.

### Epiphany Door Blessing

On January 6, many Catholic families bless the home with blessed chalk. Above the front door write the year split around the initials of the three Magi, for example **20 + C + M + B + 27**. The letters also stand for *Christus mansionem benedicat*, may Christ bless this house. Pray for all who enter in the year ahead.

### Candlemas Candle Blessing

On February 2, bring the candles you will use through the year to church for blessing, or bless them at home: set them on the altar, sprinkle them with holy water and pray that their light will guide your prayers through the year. In the craft, this is also Imbolc, Brigid's day, a time to clean the house and welcome the first light of spring.

### Oil and Water for the Evil Eye

An Italian and Mediterranean folk practice, often handed down from grandmother to granddaughter on Christmas Eve.

1. Fill a shallow white bowl with water.
2. Make the sign of the cross over it.
3. Dip a finger in olive oil and let three drops fall into the water, saying the name of the person you are praying for.
4. If the drops stay whole and round, there is no heaviness. If they spread or break apart, pray in your tradition for the heaviness to lift, and repeat until the drops hold together.
5. Pour the water down the drain.

### The Silent Supper

An old Samhain custom sometimes called the dumb supper. Set a place at the table for the ancestors, with a white candle and a plate of the food they loved. Eat the meal in silence, remembering them. Afterward, leave their plate outside overnight, or give the food to the earth.

### Diwali Lamps

On the new moon night of Diwali, clean the home thoroughly, draw rangoli at the entrance, and light rows of diyas at every door and window at dusk. Perform Lakshmi puja with flowers, sweets and coins, and keep the front door open for a time to welcome her. Stay present with the lamps and put them out before sleep.

### New Year Wax Reading

At midnight on New Year's Eve, melt a little wax from a white candle and drip it into a bowl of cold water. Look at the shape the wax makes and ask what it suggests for the year: a heart, a ring, a road, a bird, a house, a key. Write it down and look back next year.

title: Chapter 15: The Meditations of the World
md:
Meditation is the training of attention, and every tradition has developed its own way of doing it. This chapter describes the major types, where they come from, how to practice each, and what each is best for, so AMY can offer each seeker the one that fits.

### Choosing by need

| If you feel | Try first |
| --- | --- |
| Anxious or panicky | Box breathing, 4-7-8 breathing, coherent breathing, body scan |
| Scattered or restless | Breath counting, candle gazing, walking meditation, japa |
| Heavy or sad | Loving-kindness, gratitude, RAIN, gentle movement |
| Angry or hurt | Self-compassion, forgiveness, walking meditation |
| Grieving | Ancestor meditation, Rosary or Jesus Prayer, metta for the departed |
| Unable to sleep | Yoga nidra, progressive muscle relaxation, sleep body scan, 4-7-8 |
| Stuck on a decision | Ignatian examen, Lectio Divina, open awareness, journaling meditation |
| Far from God or spirit | Centering prayer, japa, dhikr, hitbodedut, adoration |
| Disconnected from your body | Body scan, yoga, tai chi, qigong standing, grounding |
| Wanting to create or attract | Visualization, new moon seed, chakra meditation |

### The map of meditation

| Type | Tradition and origin | Typical length | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Breath awareness (anapanasati) | Buddhist, from the Buddha's teaching | 5 to 30 min | Calm, focus, the foundation of all practice |
| Box breathing | Modern, used by first responders and the military | 2 to 5 min | Acute stress, steadiness |
| 4-7-8 breathing | Modern, adapted from yogic pranayama | 1 to 3 min | Sleep, anxiety |
| Alternate nostril (nadi shodhana) | Hindu yoga | 3 to 10 min | Balance, clearing the mind |
| Humming bee breath (bhramari) | Hindu yoga | 2 to 5 min | Anxiety, racing thoughts |
| Coherent breathing | Modern, about 5 to 6 breaths a minute | 5 to 20 min | Nervous system balance |
| Mindfulness (MBSR) | Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1979, from Buddhist roots | 10 to 45 min | Stress, pain, everyday awareness |
| Vipassana (insight) and noting | Theravada Buddhist | 15 to 60 min | Seeing thoughts clearly, equanimity |
| Zazen | Zen Buddhist | 10 to 40 min | Presence, discipline, stillness |
| Walking meditation (kinhin) | Buddhist | 10 to 30 min | Restlessness, grounding |
| Body scan | Buddhist roots, modern clinical use | 10 to 45 min | Tension, sleep, body awareness |
| RAIN | Tara Brach, modern Buddhist teacher | 5 to 15 min | Difficult emotions |
| Loving-kindness (metta) | Buddhist | 10 to 20 min | Warmth, healing relationships |
| Tonglen | Tibetan Buddhist | 10 to 20 min | Compassion, grief, courage |
| Self-compassion | Kristin Neff, modern | 5 to 15 min | Self-criticism, shame |
| Gratitude | Many traditions | 3 to 10 min | Mood, perspective |
| Forgiveness | Many traditions | 10 to 20 min | Old hurts, release |
| Japa (mantra repetition) | Hindu, also Buddhist and Sikh | 10 to 30 min, often 108 repetitions | Devotion, focus |
| Om chanting | Hindu, Vedic | 5 to 15 min | Stillness, vibration, prayer |
| Transcendental Meditation | Maharishi Mahesh Yogi; taught only by certified teachers | 20 min twice a day | Deep rest |
| Kirtan | Hindu bhakti, Sikh and devotional singing | 20 to 90 min | Joy, devotion, community |
| Sound bath and singing bowls | Himalayan bowls and modern sound practice | 20 to 60 min | Relaxation |
| Candle gazing (trataka) | Hindu hatha yoga | 3 to 10 min | Concentration, the Light Work nights |
| Visualization and guided imagery | Many traditions, modern psychology | 5 to 20 min | Intention, healing, confidence |
| Chakra meditation | Hindu tantra, adapted in the West | 10 to 30 min | Energy balance, self-understanding |
| Yoga nidra | Hindu yoga, modern forms by Swami Satyananda | 20 to 45 min | Deep rest, sleep |
| Dhyana | Hindu yoga, the seventh limb of Patanjali | 20 min or more | Absorption in the divine |
| Kundalini meditation | Hindu and Sikh-derived yoga | 10 to 30 min | Energy, awakening (with a teacher) |
| Qigong and standing meditation | Chinese Taoist | 10 to 30 min | Vitality, grounding |
| The inner smile | Taoist | 5 to 15 min | Kindness toward the body |
| Tai chi | Chinese martial and Taoist arts | 15 to 45 min | Moving meditation, balance |
| Yoga as meditation | Hindu | 15 to 60 min | Uniting body and breath |
| Centering prayer | Catholic, Thomas Keating and others, 1970s, from older Christian mystics | 20 min twice a day | Resting in God |
| Lectio Divina | Christian monastic, Benedictine | 15 to 30 min | Scripture, discernment |
| Ignatian contemplation | Catholic, Saint Ignatius of Loyola | 15 to 45 min | Imagining the Gospels, discernment |
| The Examen | Catholic, Saint Ignatius | 10 to 15 min | Reviewing the day with gratitude |
| The Jesus Prayer | Eastern Orthodox hesychasm | 10 to 30 min | Constant prayer, peace |
| Rosary meditation | Catholic | 15 to 25 min | Devotion, grief, steadiness |
| Christian meditation with a prayer word | Benedictine, John Main | 20 to 30 min | Silence with God |
| Taizé chant | Ecumenical, the Taizé community in France | 10 to 30 min | Peaceful sung prayer |
| Eucharistic adoration | Catholic | 15 to 60 min | Presence before the Blessed Sacrament |
| Hitbodedut | Jewish, Rabbi Nachman of Breslov | 10 to 60 min | Speaking to God in your own words |
| Dhikr | Islamic, especially Sufi | 10 to 30 min | Remembrance of God |
| Muraqaba | Sufi | 10 to 30 min | Watchful presence |
| Progressive muscle relaxation | Edmund Jacobson, early twentieth century | 10 to 20 min | Physical tension, sleep |
| Autogenic training | Johannes Schultz, early twentieth century | 10 to 15 min | Relaxation through suggestion |
| Forest bathing (shinrin-yoku) | Japan, 1980s | 20 min or more | Restoring through nature |
| Mindful eating | Buddhist, modern mindfulness | 5 to 15 min | Presence, gratitude |
| Open awareness | Tibetan Dzogchen and Mahamudra, Zen | 10 to 40 min | Spacious, effortless presence |
| Journaling meditation | Modern | 10 to 20 min | Clarity, processing |

### How to practice each

**Before any practice.** Sit in a chair with your feet on the floor, on a cushion, or lie down if the practice allows. Keep your back long and your shoulders soft. Set a gentle timer. Begin with three slow breaths. Expect the mind to wander; returning is the practice.

#### The breath

- **Breath awareness.** Rest attention on the feeling of breath at the nostrils or belly. When the mind wanders, notice where it went and return. To steady it, count breaths from one to ten and begin again.
- **Box breathing.** Breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat four to eight rounds.
- **4-7-8 breathing.** Breathe in through the nose for 4, hold for 7, breathe out through the mouth with a soft whoosh for 8. Four rounds. Stop if you feel lightheaded.
- **Alternate nostril (nadi shodhana).** Close the right nostril with the right thumb and breathe in through the left. Close the left with the ring finger, release the right, breathe out. Breathe in right, switch, breathe out left. That is one round. Continue for five to ten rounds.
- **Humming bee (bhramari).** Close the ears gently with the thumbs, close the eyes, breathe in, and on the out breath hum like a bee. Feel the vibration in the head. Five to ten rounds.
- **Coherent breathing.** Breathe in for about 5 to 6 seconds and out for 5 to 6 seconds, smoothly, with no pause.
- **Fast breathing practices** such as kapalabhati or breath-of-fire are energizing but can cause dizziness. They are not for pregnancy, high blood pressure, heart conditions, epilepsy or panic disorder, and AMY does not guide them.

#### Mindfulness and insight

- **Mindfulness.** Sit with breath, sounds and sensations, letting each come and go without holding on or pushing away. Bring the same attention to washing dishes or walking.
- **Noting (vipassana).** As each experience arises, label it softly: hearing, thinking, itching, planning, sadness. The label is gentle and brief, then attention returns to the breath.
- **Zazen.** Sit facing a wall, eyes half open, hands in a simple oval. Count breaths, or simply sit in open awareness (shikantaza), just sitting.
- **Walking meditation.** Walk slowly back and forth along a path of ten to twenty steps. Feel each foot lift, move and place. At the end, pause, turn, and walk again.
- **Body scan.** Move attention slowly from the toes to the crown, noticing each area without trying to change it. Breathe into tight places.
- **RAIN.** Recognize what is happening. Allow it to be there. Investigate with kindness where you feel it in the body. Nurture yourself with a kind word or a hand on the heart.

#### The heart

- **Loving-kindness (metta).** Silently repeat: may I be safe, may I be well, may I be at peace, may I live with ease. Then offer the same wishes to someone you love, someone neutral, someone difficult, and finally all beings.
- **Tonglen.** On each in breath, imagine breathing in the suffering of yourself or another as dark smoke. On each out breath, breathe out relief and light. Begin with your own pain, then widen to others who feel the same.
- **Self-compassion.** Place a hand on your heart. Say: this is a moment of suffering; suffering is part of life; may I be kind to myself.
- **Gratitude.** Bring to mind three specific things from the last day you are grateful for. Feel each one in the body before moving to the next.
- **Forgiveness.** Begin by asking forgiveness for any harm you have caused, then offer forgiveness to yourself, then, when you are ready, to someone who hurt you. Forgiveness never requires excusing harm or returning to an unsafe person.

#### Mantra and sound

- **Japa.** Hold a mala of 108 beads. Repeat a mantra once for each bead, moving the beads with the thumb and middle finger: Om Namah Shivaya, Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya, Om Gam Ganapataye Namah, the Gayatri Mantra, or the name of God in your tradition. Do not cross the guru bead; turn the mala and go back.
- **Om chanting.** Breathe in deeply, then chant A-U-M slowly on the out breath, letting the M hum into silence. Rest in the silence before the next.
- **Transcendental Meditation.** A specific method using a personal mantra, taught only through certified teachers for a fee. AMY can describe it but does not teach it.
- **Kirtan.** Call-and-response singing of divine names, often with harmonium and drums. Sing, then rest in the silence afterward.
- **Sound bath.** Lie down and let the tones of singing bowls, gongs or chimes wash over you. Follow one tone until it fades.

#### Concentration, imagery and energy

- **Candle gazing (trataka).** Place a candle at eye level an arm's length away. Gaze at the flame without blinking for as long as is comfortable, then close the eyes and hold the after-image between the brows. Repeat three times. Not for people with epilepsy, glaucoma or recent eye surgery. AMY's full script is in the Build Pack.
- **Visualization.** Picture a place of peace in detail, or picture your intention already fulfilled: what you see, hear and feel. End by returning to the breath.
- **Chakra meditation.** Move attention through seven centers along the spine, from the base to the crown, imagining each as a wheel of light in the colors red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, with the seed sounds LAM, VAM, RAM, YAM, HAM, OM and silence.
- **Yoga nidra.** Lying down, follow a guide through an intention (sankalpa), a rotation of attention through the body, awareness of breath, opposite sensations such as heavy and light, and imagery, resting on the edge of sleep while staying aware.
- **Dhyana.** The seventh limb of Patanjali's yoga: after the body is still and attention is gathered on one object, attention flows to it unbroken, often an image or name of the divine.
- **Kundalini meditation.** Combines breath, mantra, posture and movement to awaken energy at the base of the spine. Powerful and best learned with a teacher.
- **Qigong standing (zhan zhuang).** Stand with knees soft as if holding a large ball before the chest. Breathe low into the belly. Begin with five minutes.
- **The inner smile.** Smile softly, then imagine sending that smile to your eyes, heart, lungs, belly and every organ, thanking each.
- **Tai chi and yoga.** Slow, flowing movement joined with breath; best learned with a class or video.

#### Christian contemplative prayer

- **Centering prayer.** Choose a sacred word such as Jesus, Abba, peace or love. Sit for twenty minutes resting in God. When you notice a thought, return ever so gently to the sacred word.
- **Lectio Divina.** Read a short scripture passage slowly (lectio). Read again and notice a word that stands out (meditatio). Speak to God about it (oratio). Rest in silence (contemplatio).
- **Ignatian contemplation.** Read a Gospel scene and place yourself in it with all your senses: the dust, the voices, the face of Jesus. Notice what you feel and speak to him.
- **The Examen.** At night: give thanks for the day; ask for light; review the day hour by hour, noticing where you felt close to God and where far; ask forgiveness; look toward tomorrow with hope.
- **The Jesus Prayer.** Repeat with the breath: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God (breathing in), have mercy on me (breathing out). Use a prayer rope if you have one.
- **The Rosary.** Hold each mystery in the mind, a scene from the life of Jesus or Mary, while the Hail Marys move like breath. One decade is about four minutes; five decades about twenty.
- **Christian meditation.** Repeat the prayer word Maranatha, "Come, Lord", in four equal syllables, silently and faithfully, for twenty to thirty minutes.
- **Taizé chant.** Sing a short phrase of scripture over and over, softly, until it becomes prayer.
- **Adoration.** Sit before the Blessed Sacrament in a church or chapel. Speak, listen or simply be present.

#### Jewish and Islamic paths

- **Hitbodedut.** Go somewhere alone, ideally in nature, and speak to God aloud in your own words, as to a close friend, for a set time each day.
- **Dhikr.** Repeat a remembrance of God, such as SubhanAllah, Alhamdulillah, Allahu Akbar, or La ilaha illallah, often on prayer beads in sets of 33 or 99.
- **Muraqaba.** Sit in silence, watching the heart, aware that God is watching over you.

AMY speaks of Jewish and Islamic practices with respect and only when a seeker brings their own faith to the conversation.

#### Relaxation and everyday practice

- **Progressive muscle relaxation.** Tense a muscle group firmly for about five seconds, then release for fifteen, from the feet up to the face.
- **Autogenic training.** Repeat calm phrases about the body: my arms are heavy, my arms are warm, my heartbeat is calm and regular, my breathing is easy.
- **Forest bathing.** Walk slowly in nature with no destination, phone away, noticing smells, sounds, textures and light.
- **Mindful eating.** Eat one small food, such as a raisin or a square of chocolate, as if for the first time: look, smell, taste slowly, notice the swallow.
- **Open awareness.** Let attention rest on everything at once, sounds, sensations, thoughts, without choosing any, like the sky holding clouds.
- **Journaling meditation.** Write without stopping for ten minutes, beginning with a prompt such as: what is asking for my attention?

#### A note on difficult experiences

Meditation is safe for most people, but it can bring up strong emotions, old memories or, rarely, distressing experiences. If a practice makes you feel worse, stop, open your eyes, feel your feet on the floor and name five things you can see. People with trauma, psychosis, severe depression or a seizure disorder do best with practices that keep the eyes open and the body moving, and with the guidance of a qualified professional.

title: Chapter 16: Meditations of the Craft
md:
The craft has its own meditations, used before and after rituals to steady the practitioner, protect the spirit and open the inner senses. Each one here can be guided by AMY in three to twelve minutes.

### Grounding: the tree

Used before and after every working.

1. Sit or stand with your feet flat on the floor.
2. Imagine roots growing from the soles of your feet down through the floor, through the soil and stone, deep into the cool dark earth.
3. On each out breath, let tension, worry and excess energy drain down the roots into the earth, which receives it without harm.
4. On each in breath, draw up steady, warm strength from the earth.
5. Imagine branches rising from the crown of your head toward the sky, drinking in light.
6. Rest as the tree, rooted and reaching. When you finish, press your palms to the floor.

### Centering

Gather your attention into one point, usually just below the navel or at the heart. Breathe into it until you feel collected, as if all of you has come home.

### Shielding: the circle of light

1. Ground first.
2. Imagine a point of light at your heart. With each breath it grows until it surrounds your whole body in a sphere about an arm's length away.
3. Choose its color: white for purity, gold for strength, blue for Saint Michael's protection, violet for spiritual protection.
4. Seal it above your head and below your feet. Say: only love may enter here; what is not mine may not stay.
5. Know that the shield lets love, help and good words in, and lets your own love out.

Catholic practitioners may picture Saint Michael standing behind them with his shield. Hindu devotees may picture Hanuman or the protective presence of the Goddess.

### Releasing cords

A meditation for letting go of what still pulls at you from a past relationship, job or situation. It cuts nothing from the other person; it returns your own energy to you.

1. Ground and shield.
2. Notice where in your body you feel pulled toward the old situation. Imagine a cord of light there.
3. Thank the situation for what it taught you.
4. Imagine the cord gently dissolving into light, or being released by a guardian you trust, with the words: I take back what is mine; I return what is yours; we are both free.
5. Fill the place where the cord was with warm golden light.

### The four elements

Spend two minutes with each element.

- **Earth.** Feel your weight, your bones, the floor holding you. Earth gives stability and patience.
- **Air.** Feel the breath and the air on your skin. Air gives clarity and new ideas.
- **Fire.** Gaze at a candle or feel the warmth of your own body. Fire gives courage and transformation.
- **Water.** Imagine standing in a gentle river, or hold a glass of water. Water gives feeling, cleansing and flow.

End by asking which element you need most this week.

### Moon meditations

- **New moon seed.** In darkness, imagine planting one seed in rich soil. Name the seed as your intention. See it resting, held, waiting.
- **Waxing moon.** Watch the seed send out its first shoot. Each breath is sunlight and rain.
- **Full moon bathing.** Sit by a window where moonlight falls, or imagine it. Let silver light pour over you from the crown to the feet, filling you with gratitude for what has grown.
- **Waning moon release.** Imagine standing by the sea at night as the tide goes out. Give the water one thing you are ready to release and watch the tide carry it away.

### The crossroads

In folklore around the world, the crossroads is the place of choice and meeting. Imagine walking at midnight along a dirt road lit by the moon until you reach a crossroads. Stand at the center. Look down each road in turn and notice what you sense: a feeling, a color, a word. Ask which road is truly yours. Walk a few steps down it, then return. Write down what you received. AMY uses the crossroads image only as a symbol of choice, not as a call to any spirit.

### The inner temple and the guide

A pathworking is a guided visualization journey. Imagine a path through a forest, a stair descending into warm light, or a door in a garden wall. Behind it is your inner temple, a sacred place built from what comforts you: a chapel, a mandir, a grove, a room by the sea. Sit there and ask for a guide. Christians may meet their guardian angel or a saint; Hindus their ishta devata; others a wise elder or an animal. Ask one question and listen. Thank the guide, return the way you came, and ground.

### Meeting the ancestors

Light a white candle beside an ancestor's photograph. Imagine a long table set in a warm room. One by one, those who came before you enter and sit. Some you know; some are older than memory. Tell them what you are carrying. Listen for what they wish for you. Thank them. Watch them return to the light. Change the water on your ancestor altar afterward.

### Before divination

Ground, shield and center. Hold the cards, the glass or the pendulum. Say: may I see clearly, and may what I see serve my highest good and the good of all. Breathe three times. Then begin the reading.

### Shadow work

Shadow work means meeting the parts of yourself you have hidden or rejected: anger, jealousy, fear, need. Sit with a journal. Ask: what quality in other people irritates me most? Where does it live in me? What does that part of me want? Write without judging. End with a hand on your heart and a word of kindness to that part of yourself.

Shadow work can stir up old pain. Go slowly, stop if you feel overwhelmed, and lean on a therapist or a trusted person when the material is heavy.

### Cleansing the aura

Imagine standing beneath a waterfall of clear light. It washes from your crown down over your shoulders, chest, back and legs, carrying away anything grey or heavy into the earth. Turn slowly so it reaches every side. Step out shining.

### After every working

Ground again. Eat or drink something simple. Wash your hands. Write what you did and how you feel. The ritual is finished; return gently to ordinary life.

title: Safety
md:
Every ritual and meditation in this book is meant to leave a person safer and calmer than before. These rules apply to all of them.

### Fire

- Never leave a burning candle, diya, incense or simmer pot unattended. Put it out before you leave the room or go to sleep.
- Set every flame on a heat-safe plate, away from curtains, paper, books, hair, loose sleeves and drafts, and out of reach of children and pets.
- Trim wicks to about a quarter inch. Use only a few drops of oil and the smallest pinch of herb on a candle; too much can flare.
- Stop using a glass candle if the glass cracks, blackens heavily or gets very hot, or when about half an inch of wax remains.
- Burn paper only over a sink, in a fireproof dish, with water nearby, or choose dissolving or burying instead.
- Florida Water and other colognes are flammable. Keep them away from flame.
- Keep a fire extinguisher or a lid for smothering flame within reach.

### Herbs, oils and food

- Do not eat or drink any herb, oil or preparation that is not an ordinary kitchen food.
- Make dressing oils only with dried herbs. Fresh herbs and garlic in oil can grow harmful bacteria.
- Dilute essential oils before they touch skin, and test a small patch first. Never swallow essential oils.
- Rue, mugwort, pennyroyal, tansy and wormwood are unsafe in pregnancy; pennyroyal oil is toxic to everyone and AMY never recommends it.
- Many plants and oils are toxic to pets, including eucalyptus, tea tree, garlic, lilies and essential oil diffusers.
- Wash hands after raw egg limpias, and keep eggs away from cuts.
- Smoke cleansing should happen with a window open, and never around people with asthma or small children.

### Breath and body

- Stop any breathing practice that makes you dizzy, tingly or anxious, and breathe normally.
- Avoid fast or forceful breathing, long breath holds and inversions during pregnancy, with heart or blood pressure conditions, or with epilepsy.
- Candle gazing is not for people with epilepsy, glaucoma or recent eye surgery.

### The heart and mind

- Meditation and ritual are not therapy and do not replace medical or mental health care.
- If someone is thinking about suicide or self-harm, all ritual stops. In the United States, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or 911 in an emergency.
- If someone is being hurt or threatened at home, safety comes first: 911, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.
- No ritual, reading or candle requires a purchase to bring safety, peace or spiritual growth.
- Readings are offered for entertainment and reflection. No one can promise an outcome.
